title: Paul McCartney’s court hearing to dissolve The Beatles’ partnership – day one | 1971
content:
19 February 1971 was the first day of Paul McCartney’s court hearing to have The Beatles’ business partnership dissolved.

McCartney was the only member of the band to attend London’s Royal Courts of Justice on this day. He arrived with his wife Linda. It was their only day in attendance during the court case.

Embed from Getty Images

McCartney’s barrister, David Hirst, QC, began by restating the requests made in the 31 December 1970 filing, and again at the initial hearing on 19 January 1971: that the partnership should be dissolved, and that a receiver be appointed to oversee The Beatles’ group and individual assets.

Hirst also read out almost all of the band’s 1967 partnership agreement, and outlined the change in their partnership in the intervening years. He went through the fees charged by their business manager Allen Klein, telling the court that “our confidence in Mr Klein has not been enhanced” by his conviction the previous month on ten counts of tax fraud in New York, before adding that there was the danger of a similar outcome in the UK.

It seems that Mr Klein has demonstrated towards the United States Federal authorities a willful failure to account comparable to that demonstrated towards the partners in Beatles & Company. The U.S. tax authorities can and have invoked criminal sanctions. We are dependent upon the civil sanctions available in this Court to enforce our rights.
David Hirst, QC

Hirst told the court that one outcome of The Beatles’ legal dispute was that EMI was witholding £488,000 in royalties for the McCartney album. The record label was awaiting the court’s ruling on whether to release the money to McCartney, or to Apple, as The Beatles’ EMI contract stipulated.

McCartney also provided a 12-page affidavit, which outlined The Beatles’ business arrangements since the death of their manager Brian Epstein. It also went into detail as to how the business issues came to a head after the other three members signed a management agreement with Klein. “I never signed or ratified the agreement,” he wrote. “I never accepted Klein either as my manager or manager of The Beatles.”

Embed from Getty Images

Other sticking points in the affidavit were the disagreements over the release date of McCartney, Phil Spector’s orchestrations on ‘The Long And Winding Road’, and McCartney’s attempts to persuade the other Beatles to allow him to leave the partnership.

Paul and Linda sat in the front row of the court during the hearing, and a number of Beatles fans were in the public gallery. The other Beatles were represented by Morris Finer, QC.

A member of McCartney’s legal team had bet him 25 pence that Lennon would turn up. McCartney collected his winnings during the lunch break.
